summary: Before astronauts and rovers work on the Moon or Mars, mission teams need to know where, and what, to rehearse on Earth. TerrainX addresses NASA’s Permanent Moon Base and Mars analog challenge by comparing open NASA observations (POWER climate, SRTM, MOLA, LOLA, Diviner, SPICE) with mapped geology. It keeps three scores separate: terrain fidelity, mission utility and evidence coverage. A reproducible 130-cell search shows that ranking for the mission instead of dryness alone changes 12 of 13 Mars picks. A lunar south-pole module matches Artemis III region features to Earth relief and shows where the analogy breaks. Eight Research Lab tools turn open questions into field protocols with stations, measurements and stated limits. No score certifies an analog or predicts mission success.
details:
The original discovery screens 130 NASA POWER precipitation cells in four bounded study regions, selecting 16 geographically separated candidates and characterizing them alongside 4 independent reference benchmarks. Ten automatic candidates support preliminary hypotheses under the declared default model; none is field-verified. The expanded experiment characterizes all 130 cells with POWER point climate, SRTM terrain and available Macrostrat mapping. It has 79 rankable Mars cells and 1 lunar sampling lead under its release model. Its geographically separated Mars shortlist contains 13 cells, 12 absent from the original aridity shortlist. These are findings within this sample, not first-ever discoveries.

Terrain fidelity F is a Gaussian similarity over four terrain metrics with explicit tolerances. Utility U is a weighted mean of mission criteria, and coverage C is the share of that weight backed by evidence. A combined priority P = αF + (1 − α)U, multiplied by C^γ, is reported only when C ≥ 0.7 and geology is assessed. Missing values stay unknown, never zero. For example, Western Saudi Arabia · 02 scores F 94.7, U 66.2, C 100% and P 74.8 for Jezero Crater. The Discovery Frontier asks which next measurement could change an interpretation. Six lenses and model-sensitivity analysis show that no single ranking is universally correct. Source inspection keeps actual units, periods, response hashes (SHA-256) and observation support. A separate 18-site Copernicus/MOLA/LOLA study tests 8 and 12 km aggregation across 360 valid comparisons, while the original SRTM rankings remain identifiable.

The lunar module samples real LOLA terrain at eight IAU feature centres named in NASA’s October 2024 Artemis III region announcement. It summarizes Diviner thermal and ice-stability models, independently verified against the 604.8 MB PDS source and its published MD5, and adds SPICE-based sunlight estimates. At Haworth, 100% of the sampled area lies below the 110 K cold-trap threshold. Its closest Earth twin matches its slopes but not its relief, and the score shows that mismatch. Area weighting, undefined ice codes and air-versus-surface temperature differences are stated. Modelled stability is not detected ice, and feature centres are not landing polygons.

The Research Lab addresses what screening scores cannot. Eight tools cover:

  • mineralogy, including published Lake Salda XRD data (98.6% hydromagnesite);
  • sunlight and thermal extremes;
  • water and ice resources;
  • dust thresholds (Shao–Lu);
  • biology controls;
  • documented caves;
  • least-cost routes on 250 m Copernicus grids;
  • lunar-base power trade-offs.

Each tool separates measured, modeled and unknown evidence, then writes a field protocol.

The Field Study Builder turns that protocol into a plan on real cached terrain. It offers proposed stations, a relief transect, measurements, equipment, JSON/GPX export and a printable field book, all pinned to the science release. Full JSON keeps every field. Share links keep stations, intent and model, while compact QR links are explicitly narrower. Verified offline preparation keeps the science and exports working without external maps.
